patient.chief_complaint: Six-day progressive ascending weakness and areflexia with bilateral facial weakness, preceded by URI. SpO2 93% on room air in 68-year-old diabetic.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. N. is a 68-year-old man presenting with a 6-day history of progressive ascending weakness. He had a URI 2 weeks ago. Six days ago, foot tingling began; weakness rapidly ascended and he is now unable to walk. He has bilateral facial drooping and cannot swallow water without coughing. SpO2 93% on room air at triage. He has known mild diabetic peripheral neuropathy (distal vibration loss only) — but his new symptoms are acutely different and far more severe. This is a classic GBS case in an elderly patient with baseline mild neuropathy.

Recognize influenza A as GBS trigger — acute demyelination within weeks of influenza

key_reasoning_points: Influenza A is a well-recognized GBS trigger — influenza vaccine-associated GBS is a separate much rarer entity (~1 in 1 million)
Background mild diabetic neuropathy does NOT change GBS management — treat GBS on its own merits
